Foot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis

shoe and water exposures · persistent focal pain · MRI and bone cultures

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Nail through a shoe with persistent or returning deep foot pain weeks later: think Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, even in an otherwise well, afebrile child.
  • Plain radiograph first for bone and retained material. Normal early films do not exclude bone infection; persistent focal pain calls for MRI.
  • Confirmed deep puncture-wound infection: orthopedic treatment with debridement, bone cultures and antibiotics covering Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus. Fresh water favors Aeromonas; salt water favors Vibrio.
What it is

Infection of bone after a penetrating foot wound; nearby cartilage may also be involved

Bug

Pseudomonas aeruginosa after a shoe-sole puncture; Staphylococcus aureus remains the usual organism overall

Spread

A penetrating wound introduces organisms directly; contamination and retained material matter

Chain

Puncture inoculation persistent deep pain and inflammation bone infection

Insights

Exposure changes the organism. The same puncture has different likely pathogens through footwear, in fresh water or in seawater.

An early film can miss the infection. Radiographic changes lag, while MRI detects early disease more sensitively.

2Urgent risks
Deep infectionIncreasing focal bone pain, swelling or reduced weight bearing after a puncture

If osteomyelitis is suspected despite a normal early film, choose obtain MRI and arrange orthopedic assessment; do not wait for fever.

UnstableShock in a patient with suspected bone infection

If the patient is unstable, choose start antibiotics while arranging source control and cultures; do not delay treatment for biopsy.

4Workup
Clues that change the next step
CluePoints toNext best step
Persistent focal pain after a shoe puncturePossible deep infectionMRI if early radiographs do not explain the pain
A freshwater-contaminated woundAeromonas infection is possibleChoose antibiotics for the freshwater exposure
A possible wooden fragmentRetained radiolucent foreign bodyUse ultrasound to locate it

Pause point. Overall, staphylococci cause most osteomyelitis. The shoe puncture and delayed focal pain are the clues that move Pseudomonas ahead in this case.

1

Wound carean acute puncture

Clean the wound, assess for retained material and review tetanus immunizationWound careSimple low-risk wounds do not automatically need antibiotic prophylaxis. Risk, contamination and the exposure guide the decision; a footwear puncture can introduce Pseudomonas.

Practice
How NBME framed it

A child aged 7 has ongoing foot tenderness, redness and warmth at a follow-up visit, 3 weeks after stepping on a nail through footwear. The wound had been cleaned. Temperature is 37.2 degrees C, and the child otherwise appears well. Tetanus immunization was last given at age 5.

Which organism best fits this exposure and course?

Competing answers
  • Aeromonas hydrophila: consider contamination by fresh water or soil; neither is the distinguishing exposure here.
  • Group A streptococcus: fits superficial spreading cellulitis better than the persistent deep shoe-puncture pattern.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: lacks the characteristic footwear association.
  • Staphylococcus aureus: leads overall in bone infection; the route of injury shifts this case toward another organism.
Down to two

Pseudomonas aeruginosa versus Staphylococcus aureus. Footwear penetration followed by persistent focal pain favors Pseudomonas bone infection, despite the near-normal temperature. Recent tetanus immunization changes wound prophylaxis, not the organism.

  1. 10-year-old boy, 10 days after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel improved at first; heel pain now returning limps; mild swelling and tenderness No water exposure Afebrile · white blood cell count normal · MRI: calcaneal marrow edema → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → persistent or returning deep pain after a shoe puncture favors Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, even without fever or leukocytosis; S. aureus and streptococci cause superficial skin infection
  2. 9-year-old girl stepped barefoot on a tack on the kitchen floor 2 days ago spreading redness around the puncture warm and tender No water or soil exposure T 38.1 °C · foot radiograph normal → Staphylococcus aureus → a puncture infection in the first days is cellulitis, most often Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci; through a sneaker, persistent or returning deep pain points to Pseudomonas
  3. 15-year-old boy cut his sole on a branch while wading barefoot in a lake 1 day later: rapidly spreading painful redness foot swollen Fresh water, not the sea T 38.9 °C · HR 112/min → Aeromonas hydrophila → a fast-spreading wound infection soon after fresh-water exposure is Aeromonas hydrophila; salt water or raw shellfish points to Vibrio vulnificus
  4. 8-year-old boy, 2 weeks after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel worsening heel pain and swelling tender over the calcaneus Walks on his toes T 37.4 °C · foot radiographs normal → MRI of the foot → early radiographs are often normal in osteomyelitis; MRI is more sensitive and shows marrow edema
  5. 11-year-old girl was diagnosed with calcaneal osteomyelitis by MRI today a nail went through her sneaker 3 weeks ago heel pain and swelling persist Afebrile and otherwise well T 37.3 °C · foot film normal → Surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics → osteomyelitis after a puncture through a shoe needs surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics, plus S. aureus coverage until cultures return
Pairs with The Limping Child: a limp after a nail through a shoe routes here. Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: joint organisms by host. Diabetes Complications and Annual Care: diabetes also carries a high risk of Pseudomonas osteomyelitis.
Transferable rule

After a shoe puncture, delayed deep pain favors Pseudomonas. Early superficial cellulitis without water exposure favors S. aureus or streptococci; fresh water favors Aeromonas.
